title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: where the link stands, and what the tag really asks

questions.prompt: "therefore" is an adverb, so it may stand in more than one place inside its clause — but not in every place. In which of these four lines does it sit where English does not allow it?

options.text: The bus was full; therefore, Wassim walked to the market.
The bus was full. Wassim therefore walked to the market.
The bus was full. Wassim, therefore, walked to the market.
The bus was full. Wassim walked therefore to the market.

questions.explanation: "The bus was full. Wassim walked therefore to the market." is the line to cross out: the adverb has been pushed between the verb and what follows it, and English keeps that slot closed. It is the slot your own language uses for its own linking word, which is exactly why the mistake is so frequent. The three others show the three places English does allow: "The bus was full; therefore, Wassim walked to the market." puts it at the head of the clause, after a semicolon that closes the first one; "The bus was full. Wassim therefore walked to the market." puts it between the subject and the verb, with no commas; and "The bus was full. Wassim, therefore, walked to the market." puts it just after the subject, held between two commas.

questions.prompt: A tag only fits the statement it was built from. Which of these four openings can carry the tag "is he?" at the end?

options.text: Hichem is the new goalkeeper of the team,
Hichem isn't the new goalkeeper,
Hichem was not at the meeting,
Hichem and Rania aren't coming,

questions.explanation: "Hichem isn't the new goalkeeper," is the one: its statement is negative, so the tag must be positive; its auxiliary is is, so is comes back; and its subject is one man, so the pronoun is he. "Hichem is the new goalkeeper of the team," is positive, so its tag turns over the other way and becomes "isn't he?". "Hichem was not at the meeting," is negative and would take a positive tag, but its auxiliary is in the past, so it calls for "was he?". And "Hichem and Rania aren't coming," is negative too, but its subject is two people, so it calls for "are they?".

questions.prompt: Nizar has to ask a librarian he has never met to keep a book for him until Friday. All four sentences below are correct English. Which one fits the person he is speaking to?

options.text: Keep this book for me until Friday afternoon, will you?
You will keep this book for me until Friday.
Could you keep this book for me until Friday, please?
Let's keep this book until Friday afternoon.

questions.explanation: "Could you keep this book for me until Friday, please?" is the one: a bare imperative is perfectly normal between friends, from a teacher to a class, or on a notice, but to a stranger who owes you nothing it lands like an order, and English turns it into a question with could you and please. "Keep this book for me until Friday afternoon, will you?" softens the order with a tag, which makes it friendly rather than polite — you would say it to a classmate, not to somebody you have never met. "You will keep this book for me until Friday." uses will as an instruction given from above, the tone of somebody who has authority over the listener. And "Let's keep this book until Friday afternoon." uses let's, which puts the librarian and Nizar inside the same action, as though they were going to do it together.

questions.prompt: Read this paragraph from a school magazine, then say where its writer stands. "Nobody thinks clearly with an empty stomach: a family that cannot pay for bread and school books has been robbed of half of its choices. Yet I have watched money turn quiet men into hard ones, and I have seen brothers stop speaking over a strip of land. What decides is never the sum in the account; it is the hand that holds it."

options.text: The writer judges money by the use made of it.
The writer believes only the poor can keep their dignity.
The writer is against money in every form.
The writer says money has no effect on people at all.

questions.explanation: "The writer judges money by the use made of it." is where the paragraph lands, and its last sentence says so almost word for word: what decides is not the sum but the hand that holds it. "The writer believes only the poor can keep their dignity." invents a claim the text never makes; it says that money can harden a man, not that poverty makes anybody better. "The writer is against money in every form." ignores the whole first sentence, where the lack of money is described as taking half of a family's choices away. And "The writer says money has no effect on people at all." contradicts the middle of the paragraph, where money hardens men and divides brothers.

questions.prompt: Mouna comes home and finds the front door standing open. She turns to her brother and says: "You didn't lock the door, did you?" He did lock it before he left. Which answer does English give her?

options.text: No, I did.
Yes, I didn't.
No, I locked it before I left.
Yes, I did.

questions.explanation: "Yes, I did." is the answer: in English yes and no answer the fact, never the shape of the question. The door was locked, so the fact is positive, so the answer opens with yes and repeats the auxiliary of the tag. "No, I did." says no and then states the opposite, so the two halves of the answer fight each other. "Yes, I didn't." makes the same mistake the other way round. And "No, I locked it before I left." is the trap your own language sets, where a no is used to contradict a negative question; an English ear stops at the no and understands that the door was left open.

questions.prompt: Hedi copied his neighbour's homework for a whole term and was never caught; his marks were the best of his life. In June the examination paper was put in front of him, and he could not write four lines of it on his own. Which saying sums up his year?

options.text: Better late than never.
Cheats never prosper.
Many hands make light work.
Look before you leap.

questions.explanation: "Cheats never prosper." is the saying: the marks Hedi took without earning them looked like a gain all year and bought him nothing at all on the one day that counted, which is precisely what the proverb warns about. "Better late than never." comforts somebody who acts too late but does act in the end; Hedi never acted. "Many hands make light work." praises a task shared between several people, and copying is not sharing a task, it is having somebody else carry yours. And "Look before you leap." warns against deciding too fast; Hedi's fault was not one hasty decision but a habit he kept up for a whole term.
